ecologyNotes:
Mycorrhizal with oaks and sometimes hickories. Cap bright orange-yellow to egg-yolk yellow, larger and brighter than C. appalachiensis. Stem tapering toward the base, coloured like the cap or paler, with white basal mycelium. Flesh white, unchanging when sliced. Odor usually strong, fragrant and sweet, reminiscent of apricots. Grows alone, scattered, gregariously, densely gregariously, or in loose clusters. Summer and fall.

The undersurface is the whole point of this entry: smooth or with shallow wrinkles, occasionally with more developed wrinkles that approach creating a veined surface near the margin, and running down the stem. A player who has learned 'ridges good, gills bad' meets a chanterelle with neither.

NOTE: gills.edge is deliberately absent. A smooth hymenium has no gill edge to read, so an examination returns 'not-applicable' — which is real evidence, and is why gills.edge is no longer a discriminator in this confusion set. This resolves an earlier open question rather than leaving it.

OPEN QUESTION FOR REVIEW: spore print is recorded as 'pale-yellow' from the source's 'pale pinkish yellow'. The pinkish component is dropped because the vocabulary has no value for it, and that omission is load-bearing — it is the only character separating this species from C. appalachiensis, whose print is white to creamy. Two things to confirm: that a pale pinkish yellow print is genuinely distinguishable on paper from a white-to-creamy one, and whether the vocabulary needs a 'pinkish-yellow' value. If the answer to the first is no, this species' print should be widened to overlap and spore.print goes back to being a red herring.

OPEN QUESTION FOR REVIEW: hymenium.type is recorded as 'smooth' alone, though the source allows wrinkles that 'approach creating a veined surface'. Adding 'false-ridges' as a second value would make this species inseparable from C. appalachiensis on that character. Confirm 'smooth' alone is right.

OPEN QUESTION FOR REVIEW: phenology is encoded as June–November from 'Summer and fall'. Narrow it to the Kentucky window.
